subject: 신석기 거석 유적과 축조 노동
title: Megalithic sites and the labour they required
content: Stones weighing many tonnes were raised at sites across prehistoric Europe, and archaeologists have judged the labour involved by experiment, moving copies with ropes, rollers, and earthen ramps. The figures that come out are large but not out of reach, since a few hundred people working through several seasons could do what a single monument needed. What such figures change is the question we ask of these sites. If the labour lay within reach of a modest community, then the monuments do not require a ruler to explain them, and the older view that they prove the rise of chiefs falls away. Digging supports this change, because the settlements around many megalithic sites are small and show little gap in wealth between houses. Feasting deposits found near several monuments suggest instead that the work was drawn together by gatherings that brought scattered groups to one place. On this reading the building was itself the point rather than merely the means, since coming together to raise a stone created the ties that held a spread-out people together. Archaeologists therefore treat these sites as records of joint effort among equals rather than of command, and the shift matters because the older reading brought in a political order that the dug ground does not show.

subject: 도덕적 지위는 무엇이 부여하는가
title: What confers moral status
content: Some beings may be wronged and others may only be damaged, and moral philosophy calls the difference a matter of moral status. A person can be wronged, a painting can only be damaged, and the question is what marks the boundary. The answer matters because our treatment of animals, of infants, and of people whose capacities are impaired all depend on where it falls. Sentience is the most defended criterion, since a being whose experience can go better or worse has something at stake in how it is treated. This is intuitive and it delivers verdicts many find uncomfortable, because it extends status widely while excluding beings that lack experience altogether. Rationality is the traditional alternative, and it excludes infants and the severely impaired unless it is qualified in ways that weaken it considerably. A third approach abandons the search for a single property. On this view moral status arises from relationships rather than from features, so a creature has standing because it stands in some connection to a moral community. This accommodates our actual practice, which extends protection unevenly according to closeness, and its cost is that it appears to make status contingent on who happens to care.

subject: 동굴 퇴적층이 기록한 점유의 단절
title: Cave layers and the gaps in occupation
content: A cave floor accumulates in layers, and archaeologists read them as a sequence in which occupation alternates with abandonment. Layers rich in hearths, bone, and tools record people living there, while sterile bands of clay or roof fall record intervals when nobody did. Because such deposits build slowly and remain undisturbed, a single excavated section can span many thousands of years. What the gaps record is the interesting part. Some correspond to climatic intervals when the surrounding landscape could not support a group, and pollen preserved in the same layers confirms the change. Others show no environmental cause and must be explained by movement, since the people who used the cave had gone elsewhere for reasons the deposit cannot recover. Distinguishing these two kinds of gap is a central problem in prehistoric archaeology. Dating the layers directly has sharpened the picture considerably. Where charcoal or bone survives, the interval of abandonment can be measured rather than estimated, and several caves once thought continuously occupied turn out to hold breaks of many centuries. Historians of the prehistoric period therefore treat continuity as something to be demonstrated in each case rather than assumed from the presence of remains at the top and bottom of a sequence.

subject: 의도와 예견된 부작용의 구분
title: Intending harm and merely foreseeing it
content: A doctrine of long standing in moral philosophy distinguishes harm that an agent intends from harm she foresees without intending, and it holds that the second may sometimes be permissible where the first is not. A physician who gives pain relief that shortens life differs, on this view, from one who administers a drug in order to end it, even where the outcome and the knowledge are identical. Defenders argue that the distinction tracks something real about agency. What a person intends is part of her plan, so she would adopt other means if this one failed, whereas a foreseen side effect is not something she is trying to bring about and its absence would not disappoint her. This test does separate the cases, and it explains why we judge the two physicians differently. Critics reply that the distinction is too easily manipulated, since an agent can redescribe her intention to fit whatever the doctrine permits, and that examples can be constructed where the permitted act is plainly worse. They add that the person harmed is equally dead either way. Defenders answer that a principle vulnerable to abuse is not thereby false, and the argument continues because both sides are responding to genuine features of how we assess conduct.

subject: 중세 촌락의 경계 표지와 분쟁
title: Medieval boundary marks and the quarrels over them
content: Medieval villages marked their boundaries with stones, ditches, and named trees, and the records of disputes about those marks survive in considerable numbers. A boundary that ran through woodland or moor mattered because it decided who could graze, cut timber, or dig peat, and the resources involved were often more valuable than the arable land whose limits were rarely contested. Establishing where a line ran depended on memory rather than on documents. Communities walked their bounds at intervals, taking children along so that the route would be remembered a generation later, and elderly witnesses were called in court to say where the marks had stood. The archaeological traces of these lines survive as banks and ditches that follow no agricultural logic, and their dating confirms that many are older than the settlements they separate. What the disputes reveal is how the marks could fail. A stone could be moved, a tree could die, and a ditch could silt, so the physical record was fragile and the human record was contested. Historians reading medieval boundary cases therefore find communities arguing about the past as much as about the land, and the judgments turned on whose memory the court found credible.

subject: 이론의 단순성은 진리의 표지인가
title: Whether simplicity is a mark of truth
content: Scientists prefer simpler theories, and philosophy has asked whether this preference tracks truth or merely convenience. The question is sharp because simplicity does real work in choosing between hypotheses that fit the evidence equally well, so if it has no connection to truth then such choices rest on nothing. One defence argues that a simpler theory says more, since it rules out more possibilities and is therefore more easily refuted. A theory that survives testing while forbidding a great deal has passed a harder examination than one that forbids little, so the preference for simplicity is really a preference for testability. This is attractive and it does not obviously establish that simple theories are more often true. A second defence grounds the preference in probability. Where a complex theory requires many independent assumptions, each carrying its own risk of error, the conjunction is less likely than a simpler rival, so simplicity and probability align. Critics answer that this works only where the assumptions are genuinely independent, which is rarely established. What most philosophers now accept is that simplicity is defensible as a working rule while its deeper justification remains contested, and that the rule earns its place by results rather than by argument.

subject: 자연종은 실재하는가
title: Whether nature comes in kinds
content: Chemistry divides substances into elements, and biology divides organisms into species, and philosophy asks whether such divisions track joints in the world or merely reflect our purposes in classifying. The question matters because scientific laws are stated about kinds, so a law about a kind that we invented would be a law about our own conventions. Gold provides the standard case for realism about kinds. Everything with the relevant atomic number behaves alike in ways that no human decision arranged, so the category appears to be discovered rather than made. Its boundaries are sharp, its members share a hidden structure, and the same divisions would be found by any inquirer. Biological species resist this treatment. Populations vary continuously, boundaries shift as populations diverge, and biologists use several incompatible species concepts depending on what they are studying. Some philosophers conclude that kinds come in degrees, with chemistry near one end and biology further along, and that realism should be assessed case by case rather than settled in general. This conclusion preserves what is compelling in each example while giving up the hope of a single answer, and much recent work in the philosophy of science accepts it.

subject: 고대 항해자의 별자리 지식
title: What ancient sailors knew of the stars
content: Ancient sailors crossed open water without instruments, and reconstructing what they knew depends on indirect evidence, since navigators wrote nothing down and their knowledge passed by apprenticeship. Some of it can be recovered from the practices of communities that navigated this way into recent times, and some from the archaeological distribution of settlements that only a competent navigator could have reached. Stars supplied the primary reference. A given star rises and sets at a fixed point on the horizon for a given latitude, so a navigator who memorized a sequence of such points could hold a course through the night by steering toward each in turn as the previous one climbed too high. This requires no measurement, only a trained memory, and the sequences were taught as chants in several traditions. Daylight demanded other methods. Swell direction persists beneath local wind and can be felt through a hull, cloud formations mark unseen islands, and birds returning at dusk indicate land beyond the horizon. Archaeologists reading the ancient settlement of remote archipelagos treat these techniques as the necessary condition for what the dates show, since drift alone cannot account for the pattern of arrival.

subject: 가능세계 논의는 무엇을 말하는가
title: What talk of possible worlds accomplishes
content: Philosophers analyse necessity and possibility by speaking of possible worlds, saying that a claim is necessary when it holds in all of them and possible when it holds in at least one. This machinery has proved enormously useful, and it raises an obvious question about what these worlds are supposed to be. One answer takes them literally, holding that other worlds exist in the same sense that ours does and differ only in not being the one we inhabit. This gives the analysis a clear foundation, and almost nobody accepts it, since believing in countless concrete worlds to explain modal talk seems a heavy price for a technical convenience. A second answer treats worlds as abstract objects, perhaps maximal sets of propositions describing how things could have been. Nothing extra exists concretely, and the analysis retains its structure. Critics object that this explains possibility in terms of consistent description, which already presupposes the notion it was meant to analyse. A third position abandons analysis and treats the machinery as a model, useful for tracking inferences without claiming to say what necessity is. Most working philosophers proceed this way, using the framework while remaining agnostic about what underwrites it.

subject: 빙하기 이후 해수면 상승과 정착지 수몰
title: Rising seas and the settlements they drowned
content: Sea level rose substantially after the last glacial maximum, and the coastlines that prehistoric communities occupied now lie beneath shallow water. This means that a large part of the settlement record for those millennia is submerged, and the sites we excavate on land are the inland minority of what existed. Any account of prehistoric coastal life is therefore built on a biased sample. Underwater survey has begun to correct this. Peat layers, tree stumps, and worked flint recovered from the seabed establish that the drowned areas were inhabited, and in several places the preservation is exceptional because waterlogging protects organic material that would have decayed on land. Wooden structures, fish traps, and textiles survive in these deposits and almost nowhere else. What the submerged evidence changes is the picture of how people lived. Coastal and estuarine environments supported dense populations with rich diets, so the older reconstruction of prehistoric Europe as sparsely occupied inland forest reflected where archaeologists could dig rather than where people had been. Historians of the period now treat the drowned landscapes as a central part of the record, and the fact that most of it remains unexcavated as the largest gap in what we know.

subject: 회의주의에 답할 수 있는가
title: Whether scepticism can be answered
content: The sceptic argues that we cannot rule out being radically deceived, and that our ordinary knowledge claims therefore fail. The argument is short and its premises are hard to reject, since we plainly cannot distinguish our situation from a convincing deception by any evidence available from within it. Philosophy has responded in several ways without producing a reply that commands agreement. One response denies that ruling out every alternative is required. Knowledge demands eliminating the possibilities that are relevant, and a global deception is not relevant in ordinary contexts, so the sceptic changes the subject by raising it. Critics answer that relevance is doing suspicious work, since the possibility does not become false by being ignored. A second response attacks the sceptic's assumptions about meaning, arguing that our words refer to what causes our experience, so a systematically deceived speaker would be talking about her deception rather than falsely about the world. This is ingenious and it strikes many as too clever to settle a question about knowledge. What most philosophers now hold is that the value of the argument lies in what answering it reveals about knowledge, rather than in any prospect of refuting it outright.

subject: 분석과 종합의 구분은 유지되는가
title: Whether the analytic and the synthetic divide
content: Some statements seem true by meaning alone, such as the claim that bachelors are unmarried, while others depend on how the world happens to be. This distinction organized philosophy for a long time, since it appeared to separate what could be settled by reflection from what required investigation. A famous argument in the middle of the last century challenged it, and the challenge has not been fully answered. The argument observes that explaining analytic truth requires the notion of synonymy, that explaining synonymy requires the notion of definition, and that each candidate explanation appeals to the others in a circle. If no member of the family can be defined without the rest, then the distinction has not been made clear, however intuitive it seems. Defenders reply that intuitive distinctions need not be reducible to anything simpler, and that the demand for a non-circular definition is too strict. They point out that we apply the distinction reliably in ordinary cases. What the debate settled, whatever one concludes about the distinction itself, is that no statement is immune from revision merely because it looks true by meaning, and that consequence has shaped how philosophers treat the boundary between conceptual and empirical inquiry.

subject: 중세 수도원의 약초원과 의료
title: Monastery gardens and medieval medicine
content: Medieval monasteries kept gardens of medicinal plants, and the surviving plans of several houses show these laid out in beds beside the infirmary. Written herbals list what was grown and what each plant was held to treat, and archaeobotanical work on the soil of such gardens has confirmed the presence of species the texts name. The two lines of evidence agree closely enough that historians treat the plans as records of practice rather than as ideals. What the monastery supplied was continuity. Care of the sick was a religious obligation, so the infirmary operated whether or not anyone could pay, and the knowledge required was written down and copied rather than held by individuals. This made monastic medicine unusually durable in a period when secular practitioners left few records. Excavated cemeteries beside such houses show treated fractures and evidence of long-term care for the disabled. The limits are equally visible. The same cemeteries record diseases that no herbal could touch, and the texts prescribe with a confidence the outcomes do not support. Historians therefore describe monastic medicine as effective in nursing and unreliable in treatment, and the distinction matters for understanding what medieval patients were actually receiving.

subject: 지향성이란 무엇인가
title: How thoughts are about things
content: A thought can be about a city one has never visited, and a photograph can represent a person now dead, and philosophy calls this feature intentionality. Physical objects do not ordinarily point beyond themselves, so explaining how some states manage it has proved a central problem in the philosophy of mind. One approach grounds aboutness in causation. A state represents what reliably causes it, so a perception of a tree is about trees because trees produce such states under normal conditions. This explains simple cases and struggles with error, since a state caused by a bush on a dark night would then be about bushes rather than being a mistaken thought about a tree. A second approach appeals to function. A state represents what it has the biological role of tracking, so misrepresentation becomes malfunction and the difficulty about error dissolves. Its cost is that the account requires a history of selection, which sits awkwardly with thoughts about mathematics or about the future. A third holds that aboutness cannot be reduced at all and must be taken as basic. Each option surrenders something the others keep, which is why the problem remains open.

subject: 선사 시대 매장 자세가 말하는 신앙
title: Prehistoric burial postures and what they suggest
content: Prehistoric burials show bodies placed in postures that vary systematically between regions and periods. Some are laid extended, some crouched with knees drawn up, some seated, and the positions are consistent enough within a cemetery that they must reflect a rule rather than the accident of interment. Archaeologists therefore treat posture as evidence about belief, and they treat it cautiously. The caution is warranted because posture underdetermines meaning. A crouched burial has been read as sleep, as a return to the position before birth, and as a practical measure to fit a body into a small pit, and the excavated evidence rarely distinguishes these. Where grave goods or orientation add further information the reading narrows, and where they do not the archaeologist can establish only that a convention existed. Changes over time carry more weight than any single reading. When a cemetery shifts from crouched to extended burial within a few generations, something in the community's practice changed, and that shift can be dated and correlated with other evidence. Prehistorians accordingly build arguments from the pattern of change rather than from the meaning of any one posture, since the pattern is recoverable while the meaning generally is not.

subject: 창발은 환원을 막는가
title: Whether emergence blocks reduction
content: Water is wet and molecules are not, and this observation is often used to argue that higher-level properties emerge in a way that resists reduction to lower-level ones. Philosophy of science has examined the claim carefully, because a great deal turns on it. If emergence is real, then explanations at higher levels cannot in principle be replaced by explanations at lower ones. Much of the intuitive support for emergence dissolves on inspection. Wetness is a property of collections rather than of individuals, and nothing mysterious follows from a collection having properties its members lack, since a circle of people has a diameter while no person does. Reduction was never the claim that a molecule is wet. A stronger version of the thesis survives this reply. It holds that some higher-level regularities hold across many different lower-level arrangements, so the higher description captures a pattern that the lower one would obscure in a mass of detail. Whether this establishes emergence or merely explanatory convenience is the live question, since a pattern that could in principle be derived is not thereby independent. What both sides accept is that our actual explanations will remain multi-level whatever the metaphysics turns out to be.

subject: 기능과 오작동의 규범성
title: Function, malfunction, and the norms they imply
content: Saying that a heart is malfunctioning asserts that it is failing to do something it ought to do, and this normative element sits oddly in a biological description. Philosophy has asked where the standard comes from, since nature contains no purposes in the ordinary sense and a diseased organ is behaving exactly as its physical state requires. The standard answer appeals to selection history. A trait has the function of doing whatever its ancestors did that explains why it was retained, so a heart that fails to pump is failing at what hearts were selected for. This grounds the norm in a historical fact and requires nothing beyond ordinary causation. Its difficulty is that history may not settle present cases, since a trait can persist for reasons unrelated to its original effect. An alternative appeals to statistical normality, treating a malfunction as a departure from what is typical for the organism's kind and stage. This handles present cases directly, and it delivers awkward verdicts where a condition is widespread, since a common impairment would count as normal. Medicine uses both notions without reconciling them, and the disagreement matters wherever calling something a disorder carries consequences for treatment or for standing.

subject: 중세 유럽의 삼림 이용권과 촌락
title: Medieval woodland rights and village life
content: Medieval woodland was rarely wilderness, and the documents recording its use describe a resource divided by right rather than by ownership. One party might hold the timber, another the right to pasture pigs beneath it, a third the right to cut underwood on a cycle, and a fourth the right to take fallen branches. These entitlements attached to households or to offices, and they could be inherited or disputed separately. The archaeology confirms that the woods were managed rather than left alone. Coppice stools of great age survive where stems were cut repeatedly on a rotation, boundary banks separate the areas held under different rights, and pollen sequences show the species composition shifting as management favoured some trees over others. A wood under this regime looks nothing like an unmanaged one, and the difference is visible on the ground today. What the arrangement supplied was predictability. A village that knew its rotation could plan the fuel and building material available in a given year, and the rules restricted taking so that the resource renewed. Historians therefore read medieval woodland rights as a working solution to a problem of shared use, and their breakdown as one cause of the clearance recorded in later centuries.

subject: 통계적 증거와 개별 사안의 판단
title: Statistics and the individual case
content: A court will not convict on statistical evidence alone, even where the statistics are overwhelming. If ninety-nine of a hundred people in a yard were trespassing, that fact does not justify a verdict against any particular one, whereas far weaker eyewitness testimony would. Philosophy has asked why, since the probability may be higher in the statistical case. One explanation appeals to a difference in how the evidence relates to the fact. Testimony, if true, is caused by the event it reports, so believing it puts one in contact with what happened, whereas a statistic would support the same conclusion whether or not this individual acted. The evidence does not discriminate between the person before the court and anyone else in the reference class. A second explanation is moral rather than epistemic. Convicting on a base rate treats a person as a member of a group rather than as an individual, and it offers her no way to distinguish herself from the class, which denies something a legal process owes her. Both explanations have force, and they come apart in cases where discrimination is possible but the accused cannot afford to establish it.

subject: 초기 인류의 불 사용 증거
title: Evidence for the earliest use of fire
content: Establishing when human ancestors began using fire is difficult because a hearth and a natural burn leave similar traces, and the deposits in question are very old. Archaeologists therefore look for signatures that wildfire cannot produce, among them clustered burnt bone, heated stone tools, and sediment altered at temperatures a brush fire does not sustain. Microscopic analysis of ash structure adds a further check. The earliest accepted evidence pushes controlled use far back, and the claims older than that remain contested rather than refuted. What makes the question important is what fire enabled. Cooking releases more energy from the same food and reduces the effort of chewing, and some researchers argue that this shift accounts for anatomical changes in teeth and gut visible in the fossil record. Fire also extended the usable day and made cold environments habitable. The archaeological difficulty is that habitual use and occasional use look different in the record. A site with hearths in every layer shows people who could make fire, whereas scattered burning may show people who exploited it when they found it. Distinguishing these is the current focus, and the answer bears directly on when the accompanying anatomical changes should be expected.

subject: 모형은 어떻게 세계를 재현하는가
title: How a model represents the world
content: Scientists work with models that are known to be false, describing frictionless planes, infinite populations, and perfectly rational agents, and yet these models explain and predict. Philosophy of science asks how something false can do that work, since a description that misdescribes its target seems poorly placed to tell us about it. One account holds that a model is not a claim about the world at all but an object in its own right, constructed to be studied and then compared with a target. The comparison is what carries content, and the claim asserted is a similarity in specified respects rather than a description. This explains why falsity is not fatal, since nobody asserted that planes are frictionless. A second account treats models as licences for inference, so that a good model lets a user draw conclusions that hold approximately in the target. Both accounts must explain how the respects and degrees of similarity are fixed, and the usual answer appeals to the purpose at hand. That answer makes representation dependent on interests, which some find unsatisfying, and it fits how modelling is actually practised.

subject: 직관은 철학의 자료인가
title: Whether intuitions are evidence
content: Philosophers describe cases and report what strikes them as true, and these judgments are then treated as data against which a theory is tested. Some hold that such intuitions are the field's evidence, much as observation is in the sciences, whereas others see the practice as a habit that philosophy would do better to drop. Defenders point out that the alternative is unclear. Rejecting intuitions outright would leave no place to begin in moral or conceptual work, since every argument must start from claims that seem true without further support. On this view intuitions are starting points that can be given up rather than reports that cannot be wrong, and they work much as ordinary perception does. Critics answer with evidence about how intuitions shift. Responses to the same case vary with wording, with the order in which cases come, and across groups, which is not how sound evidence behaves. Defenders reply that perception varies in the same way and stays evidence once its faults are known, so the right answer is to calibrate rather than to reject. Much recent work therefore tests which intuitions hold steady and which are artefacts, and that has become a research programme rather than a quarrel about whether the practice is fair.

subject: 중세 유목민의 이동식 주거
title: Portable dwellings of the medieval steppe
content: Communities on the medieval steppe lived in dwellings built to be dismantled, carried, and raised again, and the design that emerged solved several problems at once. A lattice frame expanded like a concertina, a ring at the apex held roof poles in compression, and felt covers provided insulation that could be added or removed with the season. The whole could be raised in an hour by a few people. Archaeological traces are correspondingly faint. A camp used for weeks leaves hearths, refuse, and sometimes a ring of stones that weighted the covers, but no foundations, so such sites are found by survey rather than by excavation of obvious mounds. Where the ground was frozen or arid, the traces survive better, and systematic survey has located far more of them than earlier work assumed existed. What the dwelling implies about social organization has been debated. Its size limits a household, its portability limits possessions, and the arrangement of a camp reflects seniority in ways that visitors recorded. Historians reading medieval accounts alongside the survey evidence treat the dwelling as a constraint that shaped how these communities could accumulate, since wealth had to travel or be converted into animals.

subject: 언어 행위와 약속의 힘
title: Saying and doing
content: Some utterances describe the world and others change it, so that saying the words of a promise creates an obligation that did not exist a moment earlier. Philosophy of language calls these speech acts, and their study begins from the observation that such utterances are neither true nor false but successful or defective. A promise made insincerely is not a false statement; it is a promise that fails in a particular way. What makes such acts work is a background of conventions and expectations. A person cannot promise unless there is a practice of promising, cannot name a ship unless authorized, and cannot sentence anyone unless she holds an office. The utterance draws its force from arrangements outside itself, and the conditions for success can be listed for each type of act. This has moral consequences that are easy to overlook. Because the force depends on shared conventions, someone who is not recognized as a participant may say the words without performing the act, and cases where a person's testimony is discounted or her refusal not registered are failures of this kind. Philosophers have argued that such failures are injustices rather than mere misunderstandings, since what is denied is the standing to act through speech.
